content:
In a new study, Apple researchers detailed SimpleDesign, a streamlined artificial intelligence model capable of simultaneously generating protein sequences and structures. Details are as follows.

Some background

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled 《SimpleFold: Folding Proteins is Simpler than You Think》, detailing a simplified approach for predicting protein three-dimensional structures from amino acid sequences.

In short, SimpleFold uses a flow-matching model to directly generate protein three-dimensional structures from amino acid sequences.

We have explained the principles of flow matching in more detail here, but simply put, the technique starts from a noisier random starting point and learns a relatively direct path to the final result. This contrasts with diffusion models, which typically achieve the final output through repeated denoising.

These two techniques are most commonly (or at least historically) associated with image generation, though researchers (including those at Apple) have also explored applying diffusion models to text and code generation.

Returning to SimpleFold, Apple essentially combined flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (commonly used in text generation), enabling the model to bypass some of the more computationally expensive techniques typically used by protein folding models (such as DeepMind's renowned AlphaFold).

Now, Apple researchers have introduced SimpleDesign, applying the same pursuit of simpler, general-purpose architectural concepts explored in SimpleFold to the broader protein design problem—not merely predicting protein three-dimensional structures.

SimpleDesign

As Apple's researchers explained in a new study titled 《SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign》:

In other words, while many existing protein design models rely on multi-stage pipelines, SimpleDesign learns to generate amino acid sequences and continuous three-dimensional structures in a single end-to-end training process.

Many existing protein joint design models work as follows: First, they train a separate model to convert protein structures into discrete representations or so-called "tokens." Then, they train a generative model to process these representations to generate new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips this intermediate step, learning directly from paired amino acid sequences and three-dimensional coordinates, without first compressing protein structures into another independent tokenised representation.

Apple researchers trained SimpleDesign in a rather interesting way.

They started with over 2 million protein sequence-structure pairs, primarily drawn from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold database along with other samples.

During training, they perturbed both parts of each data pair: amino acids in the sequences were randomly hidden behind mask tokens, while the corresponding three-dimensional structures had noise added.

The researchers also adjusted the degree of disruption on both sides. If the sequence was roughly intact but the structure was severely damaged, the task resembled protein folding, and the model had to recover the structure from the known sequence.

Conversely, if the structure was roughly intact but the sequence was heavily masked, it resembled inverse folding. At this point, the model had to generate a sequence capable of producing the given structure.

And when both were partially disrupted, the model learned to handle both problems simultaneously, effectively training for protein joint design.

According to the study, SimpleDesign achieved competitive results on benchmarks including protein joint design, structure generation, and sequence generation, despite a much simpler training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign was capable of generating reasonable protein structures, and the amino acid sequences it produced were overall no worse than—and in some cases superior to—those generated by most competing multimodal models.

Finally, the researchers noted that SimpleDesign's results are currently limited to in-silico evaluations, because the generated proteins have not yet been experimentally tested to confirm that they can indeed fold, function, or operate safely in real biological systems.

Nonetheless, the results are rather encouraging, and the entire study (which naturally explores SimpleDesign's architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results in greater depth) is well worth a read.
